Testimony of the Maine Snowmobile Association Neither for Nor Against LD 1762 An Act to Protect Recreational Trails by Establishing the Trails for the Future Program May 6, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the committee, my name is James Cote and I am here to testify neither for nor against LD 1762 which proposes to establish a Trails for the Future Program.
With more than 280 snowmobile clubs and thousands of miles of snowmobile trails statewide, our association is laser-focused on finding more maintenance and development resources for these clubs which supports a snowmobiling and winter industry that contributes hundreds of millions of dollars to Maine's (rural) economy.
While we are greatly appreciative of the intent and effort behind this legislation, we believe that some important considerations should be addressed before its passage:
Sec. 2, 1.- Fund established. Does this envision moving current trails bond funding into the Trails for the Future fund, or does this envision becoming a host account for future bond funding?
Sec. 2, 4.- Matching funds. We read this section to require a 50/50 matching fund, which may be extremely difficult for local snowmobile clubs to achieve and is a significantly higher matching threshold than other current funding streams.
Sec. 3, 2. Review panel. We believe that this panel could use more definition and direction to ensure that review panel membership represents a diverse group of trail stakeholders.
Sec. 3, 6. Right of first refusal. Careful consideration should be paid to how this provision should work and potential unintended consequences. Would this provision burden landowners who are otherwise willing to locate trails on their property? Would this provision burden landowners from future sale, or would it create diminished value due to the encumbrance? Private landowners are vitally important partners in Maine's snowmobile trail system and we must ensure that programs work as well for them as they do for clubs for long term success.
Lastly, we would ask if there are administrative redundancies between LD 1762 and the current Land for Maine's Future program. We would encourage the committee to evaluate those potential redundancies, and if interested in moving forward, identify ways

to harmonize the two entities, or perhaps even augment efforts at the current Land for Maine's Future program to achieve a greater focus on trails.
Again, we are always appreciative of efforts to fund trail needs in Maine and we are happy to participate in this discussion going forward. We believe, however, that any new efforts to do so must work for agencies, landowners, and clubs/users alike or we risk losing support for additional resources in the future.
Thank you for your consideration and we are pleased to answer any questions or provide more information for the work session at your request.
192808:
Testimony of John Raymond, Public Relations Representative for ATV Maine
Testimony In Support Of
LD 1762, An Act to Protect Recreational Trails by Establishing the Trails for the Future Program
Honorable Members of the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee,
My name is John Raymond, and l am the Past President and current Public Relations Representative for
ATV Maine, the statewide organization representing over 60 ATV clubs and thousands of riders across Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony in support of LD 1762, "An Act to Protect
Recreational Trails by Establishing the Trails for the Future Program," which aims to protect public access to recreational trails.
Recreational trails are a cornerstone of Maine's outdoor recreation economy, drawing visitors from near and far to explore our state's natural beauty. These trails fuel local businesses----hotels, restaurants, and outfitters--in rural areas, creating jobs and fostering community vitality. From the rolling hills of York County to the forests of Franklin County and on to the farmlands of Aroostook, ATV trails connect people to Maine's landscapes, generating economic activity that strengthens our state. However, the success of these trails depends on the trust and cooperation between trail users and the private
landowners who generously allow access to their property.
LD 1762 directly supports this critical relationship by establishing mechanisms to protect trail access while respecting landowner interests. The Trails for the Future Program, administered by the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, will acquire property or establish easements to ensure permanent public access to established recreational trails, including those used by ATVs. The bill's requirement that trails maintain their existing uses--including ATV access--safeguards the integrity of our trail network.
The economic benefits of ATV trails extend beyond tourism, supporting Maine's rural way of life. By investing in trail protection through the Trails for the Future Fund, LD 1762 will enhance the accessibility and quality of our trails, attracting more riders and amplifying their economic impact. This bill is a
proactive step to preserve the trails that drive prosperity in our communities, ensuring that future
generations of Mainers and visitors can experience the joy of ATV riding.
We commend Representative Blier and the bill's co-sponsors for their leadership in championing Maine's recreational heritage. We urge the Committee to pass LD 1762 and stand ready to answer
questions or provide further insights. Thank you for your commitment to Maine's trails and economy.
Sincerely,
John Raymond ATV Maine

motorized trails, we believe the bill's intent can be accomplished through existing provisions of the Land for Maine's Future Program and the new Maine Trails Program funded through the

This bill proposes a new program jointly administered by the Land for Maine's Future (LMF)

Branch Rail Trail) and proposes powers already existing within LMF's current authority. The
Right of First Refusal provision could also unintentionally burden land values without providing proportional benefits.
Another new element in the bill, proposed under �1892-A, section 7, permits the purchase of
rights that can later be extinguished. Currently, 12 MRS 598-A would make termination
problematic, as it would require 2/�. legislative approval to `reduce' state-owned land. The bill goes further to require that all terminations (of any interest) be subject to the Commissioner first determining there is no public purpose left (which is a high bar), followed by a judicial process.

Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker, and esteemed members of the Agriculture
Conservation and Forestry Committee.
I am Representative Mark Blier and I represent House District 138 which includes the towns of
Buxton, Cornish, Limington, and Hollis.
I'm here today to present my bill LD 1762 "An Act to Protect Recreational Trails by
Establishing the Trails for the Future Program" This bill protects an over $1 billion industry
of trail systems which provides ATV and snowmobile access in this great state.
In the early 90S, I moved from northern Maine to southern Maine to the town of Old Orchard
Beach. At that time I was able to ride my snowmobile from Old Orchard Beach all way to
Buxton. Somewhere in the mid-90s, a housing development was developed in the middle of the
trail. This closed off access partway to that destination, which was never to be opened again. We are fortunate in this state that landowners allow ATV and snowmobile clubs access to their land
to give us recreation for the benefit of our enjoyment and a huge tax collection through hotel and rental housing, restaurants, recreational vehicle dealerships, and the like.
This bill would help solidify the future access to these trails by creating a program that would buy the rights to keep trails intact for future use. This can be done through easements, but there's no particular program that would incorporate all trail systems in our state. This also will give the
option of a person who purchases the property with a trail right on it to have the availability to move the trail with the club's permission. The permission would only ensure that the relocation of the trail would not hinder snow, grooming, and or enviromnental issues. The relocation of the trail would come at the expense of the owner, but would give him the availability as long as he
connects the trail from point A to point B. There are hundreds of miles of trails within our State.
Let's work together to insure the future sustainability of a huge economic impact to our state and solidify the trails for future generations to come.
Thank you, and I am will to answer any questions.

House District 138 Cornish, Limington, Buxton (Part) & Hollis (Part)

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and distinguished members of the .

Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry. My name is Pete Didisheim. I
am the Advocacy Director for the Natural Resources Council of Maine, and I appreciate

NRCM strongly supports measures to protect public access to trails for non-motorized
and motorized uses, including snowmobiling and all-terrain vehicles. Maine has
extraordinaiy trails which contribute enormously to our economy and our way of life.

Development pressures across Maine are putting trails at risk. This bill is designed to help protect such trails through a program that would use public and private funding to protect public access to established recreational trails.

As demonstrated at the ballot box last November, Maine people strongly support investing in Maine trails of all types. The $30 million Maine Trails Bond (Question 4)
passed with 55% of the vote -- the highest margin of the three bonds on the ballot. The
Bureau of Parks and Lands has already opened the process for awarding the first $7.5 million in Maine Trails Bond grants and is conducting workshops statewide describing the program for potential applicants.

Although it_is not intended to be the primary purpose of the program, the Maine Trails Bond will allow organizations to request funding "to ensure public access through acquisition of easements or fee simple title." However, because individual grants from the Maine Trails Bond will likely be no larger than $200,000, this source of funding would not be sufficient for significant acquisitions of property or easements.

The Land for Maine's Future Program also provides important support for protecting
access to trails, and LMF projects have protected hundreds of miles of trails for non-
motorized and motorized access.

But the LMF program has run out of money, so it will not be able to support new trail
access acquisitions,'as prioritized by LD 1762, unless the Legislature provides funding
in this year's budget (such as through LD 593), or by placing an LMF bond on the ballot (as called for by LD 362).

In considering LD1762, the Committee also should be aware of two bills under consideration in the |F&W Committee. LD 1308 (sponsored by Sen. Baldacci), and LD 1441 (sponsored by Senator Black) would create working groups to study the future of public access to recreationaltrails and to identify strategies and solutions.

From our conversations with ATV and snowmobile groups, it's clear to us that the state does need to do more, and quickly, to protect public access to existing trails before access is lost forever. For many trails, it's already too late.

LD 1762 helps elevate the conversation about the risks Maine faces if public access to recreational trails is not addressed. The question for the Committee, and perhaps for
any study process that may be established, will be whether creating a new program is
the right next step for protecting trails and trail corridors while there's still an opportunity to do so.

l appreciate the opportunity to share these comments and would be glad to answer any

questions you may have.

10050762:
Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Support for
LD 1762 - An Act to Protect Recreational Trails by Establishing the Trails for the Future Program
May 6, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and esteemed members of the Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am here on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's Legislative Policy Committee (LPC) in support for LD 1762 An Act to Protect Recreational Trails by Establishing the Trails for the Future Program.
An important strength of this bill is the degree to which it supports and makes primary that the funds will be provided based on the robustness of the community engagement to establish trails and support effective protection and management of recreational trails. Section 1982-A(4) of the proposed legislation ensures that any alterations to protect trails must be approved by the local clubs or groups responsible for their maintenance regardless of the type of recreational activity. This provision continues the best practice by allowing those who know these trails best have a voice that is not only heard but instrumental in shaping future decisions.
Additionally, the bill honors community knowledge and investment with fostering shared responsibility which will enhance the long-term sustainability of trail programs, prevents top down decision making that might otherwise overlook the nuances of local trail use, cultural significance, and other practical concerns. Transparency and collaborative approaches with full accountability are vital to address use concerns and grow trail access for all types of users. Local support is crucial to protection activity and selecting based on the amount of community support that exists for the preservation of trails is not only logical, it provides thoughtful and balanced framework that honors community democracy and stewardship.
For all of these reasons, officials support the program as designed by LD 1762 and thank you for keeping these important locally led elements of evaluating grant recipients on proposed trail protection and investment.
